standard.title: Urbanisation and its impacts
standard.description: causes of urbanisation and its impacts on places and environments, drawing on a study from a country such as the United States of America, and its implications
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explain factors that influence where people live including liveability and environmental quality (AC9HG7K05), and strategies to enhance liveability (AC9HG7K08). They have not yet examined urbanisation as a process with causes and spatial impacts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the causes of urbanisation and its impacts on places and environments, drawing on a country study, and explain the implications of these impacts.

nodes.label: Urban growth vs urbanisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between urban growth and urbanisation, and explain push-pull forces that drive population movement toward urban areas.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define and distinguish urban growth from urbanisation, and identify at least two push-pull factors.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the difference between urban growth (increase in the size of an urban area) and urbanisation (increase in the proportion of population living in urban areas), and explain how push-pull forces contribute to internal and international population movements that drive urbanisation.
wider: Examine how the relative weighting of push vs pull factors differs between internal and international migration contexts.
Compare urbanisation trajectories in a developed country (USA) and a developing country, identifying structural differences.
Investigate how digital connectivity is changing the traditional push-pull model of urbanisation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate urban growth with urbanisation, or treat population movement as purely economic, will produce shallow explanations of urbanisation impacts. The conceptual distinction and the push-pull model underpin all subsequent analysis in this standard.

response_modes.reason: The urban growth / urbanisation distinction requires clear definitional work, and the push-pull model needs systematic unpacking so students can apply it analytically rather than listing factors without structure.

success_criteria: Correctly distinguishes urban growth from urbanisation with examples of each.
Identifies and categorises at least two push factors and two pull factors driving urbanisation.

nodes.label: Scales of urbanisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can distinguish between large cities and megacities, and explain urban corridor formation, drawing on examples at the national scale.
nodes.minimum_width: Students define megacity and distinguish it from a large city, with at least one located example.
nodes.typical_width: Students distinguish between large cities and megacities (population ≥10 million), describe their growth patterns and explain urban corridor formation (e.g., Boston–Washington corridor), drawing on Australian capital city growth and a US case study.
wider: Compare megacity growth patterns in the Global North (e.g., Los Angeles) with those in the Global South (e.g., Lagos, Mumbai).
Investigate what problems emerge specifically at megacity scale that are not present in large cities.
Examine urban corridor formation as a distinct urban form — what drives it and what are its infrastructure implications?
success_criteria: Defines megacity and names at least one example, explaining what distinguishes it from a large city.
Locates urban settlements at the national scale and describes the broad pattern of urban concentration.

nodes.label: Economic conditions and urban change
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how changes in economic conditions affect the characteristics of urban places, including growth, decline and renewal.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain one way that economic conditions have changed the characteristics of an urban place.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how economic conditions (tourism boom, resource decline, deindustrialisation, urban renewal investment) affect the characteristics of urban places, using examples of population growth in coastal communities, decline in regional areas, and urban renewal districts.
wider: Compare the urban character of a growth community and a declining community in the same country.
Examine gentrification as an economic-urban process — its causes and the differential effects on existing residents.
Investigate how government policy (infrastructure investment, zoning) shapes economic-driven urban change.

response_modes.reason: Using multiple economic scenarios — growth, decline, renewal — prevents students from treating economic urbanisation as only a growth story and builds capacity to explain divergent urban trajectories.

success_criteria: Explains how at least one economic condition has changed the characteristics of a named urban place.
Identifies whether the economic change produced growth, decline or transformation in the urban place.

nodes.label: Impacts of urbanisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how urbanisation produces positive and negative impacts on the quality of the environment and on economic and social opportunities.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least one positive and one negative impact of urbanisation.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain the connections between urbanisation and economic and social opportunities (university access, employment, cultural infrastructure) and the negative environmental impacts (increased carbon emissions, water consumption, habitat loss, impervious surface expansion), drawing on a country study.
wider: Examine how urban environmental impacts are unevenly distributed across different communities within a city.
Compare the environmental footprint of high-density and low-density urban forms.
Investigate how the scale of urbanisation (megacity vs regional city) changes the nature and severity of environmental impacts.

response_modes.reason: Students need to integrate economic opportunity explanations (Node 3) with environmental impact analysis to produce a balanced, multi-factor account of urbanisation's implications — the full demand of this descriptor.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The tension between urbanisation as opportunity-generator and environmental cost-producer is a genuinely complex geographic argument. Wider students can develop nuanced judgements about under what conditions urbanisation is net-positive or net-negative.
success_criteria: Explains at least two types of impact of urbanisation (economic, social or environmental) using evidence from a country study.
Distinguishes between positive and negative impacts of urbanisation on the quality of environment.
